options.a: Decoding every letter accurately but reading slowly
options.b: Self-correcting a miscue that disrupts meaning
options.c: Using context/guessing rather than decoding accurately
options.d: Showing mastery of the 'ou' vowel team and final silent e

distractorExplanations.a: Reading 'home' for 'house' is a substitution error, so the student is not decoding every letter accurately.
distractorExplanations.b: No self-correction occurred and the substitution keeps the meaning; it shows reliance on context over the print.
distractorExplanations.d: Reading 'home' for 'house' skips the 'ou' vowel team, so it shows inaccurate decoding rather than mastery.

options.a: At independent level so students can read without help
options.b: At frustration level to push students to grow faster
options.c: At grade level for every student in the class
options.d: At instructional level where students need some support

distractorExplanations.a: Independent-level text needs no teacher support, so it suits free reading; guided reading targets instructional level.
distractorExplanations.b: Frustration-level text (below about 90% accuracy) overwhelms students; guided reading uses instructional-level text.
distractorExplanations.c: Guided reading groups are leveled by each student's needs, so one grade-level text for everyone defeats the purpose.

options.a: What is this mostly about? What point does the author make?
options.b: Which sentence in the paragraph contains the most descriptive details?
options.c: What happens first, next, and last in the paragraph?
options.d: What does the first sentence say, word for word?

distractorExplanations.b: Descriptive details support the main idea; the most detailed sentence is often a supporting detail, not the point.
distractorExplanations.c: That question targets sequence; main idea asks what the paragraph is mostly about and the author's central point.
distractorExplanations.d: The main idea is not always in the first sentence and should be stated in the reader's own words, not copied.

options.a: Copying dictionary definitions and memorizing them for a quiz
options.b: Definitions, examples, non-examples, and practice in context
options.c: Weekly spelling lists tested without discussing meanings
options.d: Incidental exposure through independent reading alone

distractorExplanations.a: Copying definitions without discussion or use gives shallow knowledge; explicit instruction adds examples and practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Spelling tests target orthography, not meaning; explicit vocabulary instruction teaches meanings with examples.
distractorExplanations.d: Wide reading builds vocabulary incidentally, but explicit instruction directly teaches meanings with examples and practice.

options.a: Comprehension measured by literal recall questions
options.b: Decoding ability measured with nonsense words
options.c: Prosody (expression appropriate to meaning)
options.d: Phonemic awareness (hearing individual sounds)

distractorExplanations.a: Comprehension is the goal fluency supports, but the third fluency component is prosody, reading with expression.
distractorExplanations.b: Nonsense-word decoding measures phonics skill; the components of fluency are accuracy, rate, and prosody.
distractorExplanations.d: Phonemic awareness is an oral foundational skill; the third component of reading fluency is prosody (expression).

options.a: A flow chart showing the sequence of story events
options.b: A story map of characters, setting, problem, and solution
options.c: A cause-and-effect chain linking events to their results
options.d: A Venn diagram or T-chart listing similarities and differences

distractorExplanations.a: Flow charts suit sequence or process texts; compare-contrast needs a Venn diagram or T-chart for likenesses and differences.
distractorExplanations.b: Story maps organize the narrative elements of one text; comparing two things calls for a Venn diagram or T-chart.
distractorExplanations.c: Cause-effect chains show why events happen; compare-contrast organizers display similarities and differences.

options.a: How individual sounds blend to form spoken words
options.b: How prefixes, suffixes, and roots change word meaning
options.c: How syllables divide by vowel and consonant patterns
options.d: How sentences are combined using conjunctions

distractorExplanations.a: Blending sounds is phonemic awareness; morphological awareness concerns meaningful word parts like prefixes and roots.
distractorExplanations.c: Syllable division (VC/CV) is a phonics and decoding skill; morphology deals with meaning units, not syllable breaks.
distractorExplanations.d: Sentence combining is syntax; morphological awareness is about how affixes and roots change a word's meaning.

options.a: Measure silent reading comprehension with a test
options.b: Assign a norm-referenced grade-equivalent score
options.c: Analyze miscues and self-correction strategies
options.d: Count words read correctly per minute only

distractorExplanations.a: Running records are taken during oral reading, not silent reading; they capture miscues and self-corrections.
distractorExplanations.b: Running records are informal formative tools; they do not produce norm-referenced or grade-equivalent scores.
distractorExplanations.d: Words correct per minute is a fluency probe; running records go further, analyzing miscue types and self-corrections.

options.a: A single careful reading followed by a written summary
options.b: Extensive pre-reading lectures on the text's historical background and author
options.c: Reading a simplified summary in place of the original text
options.d: Multiple readings focusing on structure, vocabulary, and author's purpose

distractorExplanations.a: Close reading requires rereading the text several times; one pass plus a summary is surface-level comprehension.
distractorExplanations.b: Heavy front-loading replaces the text's own evidence; close reading has students reread to analyze the text itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Close reading works with the complex original text; replacing it with a simplified summary removes the analysis.

options.a: Multisensory practice and repeated exposure
options.b: Phonics rules applied letter by letter to each word
options.c: Guessing from picture cues and context alone
options.d: Postponing them until decoding skills are mastered

distractorExplanations.b: Irregular words like 'said' break regular letter-sound patterns, so letter-by-letter phonics alone misleads students.
distractorExplanations.c: Picture and context guessing is a three-cueing habit; irregular words need repeated, multisensory exposure to print.
distractorExplanations.d: High-frequency words appear constantly in early texts, so they are taught from kindergarten rather than postponed.

options.a: A retelling of every event in the exact order that it happened
options.b: Key characters, setting, problem, and resolution concisely
options.c: The reader's opinion of the characters and ending
options.d: The theme stated as a moral, without plot details

distractorExplanations.a: A full retelling includes too much detail; a summary condenses the story to its essential elements.
distractorExplanations.c: Opinions belong in a response or review; a summary objectively reports characters, setting, problem, and resolution.
distractorExplanations.d: Theme is the underlying message; a fiction summary covers the key story elements, not just a moral.

options.a: English immersion with home languages discouraged in class
options.b: Simplified texts with all academic vocabulary removed
options.c: Visual supports, cognates, and structured oral language practice
options.d: Grade-level texts assigned without visual or language scaffolds

distractorExplanations.a: Discouraging the home language discards a resource; L1 literacy and cognates transfer and support English reading.
distractorExplanations.b: Stripping academic vocabulary limits growth; ELs need access to grade-level language with scaffolds, not its removal.
distractorExplanations.d: Without scaffolds, grade-level text is often inaccessible to ELs; visuals and oral practice bridge the gap.

distractorExplanations.a: Denominator changed incorrectly.
distractorExplanations.b: Not equivalent.
distractorExplanations.c: Reciprocal not equal.

options.a: 40 cm²
options.b: 13 cm²
options.c: 26 cm²
options.d: 80 cm²

distractorExplanations.b: Perimeter mistake (13 is 5+8).
distractorExplanations.c: Doubled sum not area.
distractorExplanations.d: Calculation error.

distractorExplanations.a: Added instead of subtracted.
distractorExplanations.c: Arithmetic error.
distractorExplanations.d: Close but wrong.

options.a: 14 inches
options.b: 49 inches
options.c: 28 inches
options.d: 7 inches

distractorExplanations.a: 2 × side only.
distractorExplanations.b: Area calculation.
distractorExplanations.d: One side only.

distractorExplanations.a: Smaller than 1/2.
distractorExplanations.b: Smaller.
distractorExplanations.c: Smallest.

distractorExplanations.a: Would round down if tens were 0-49.
distractorExplanations.c: Nearest ten not hundred.
distractorExplanations.d: Not standard hundred rounding.

distractorExplanations.a: 3 pencils.
distractorExplanations.b: 5 pencils.
distractorExplanations.c: Added dollar incorrectly.

options.a: Encyclopedia entries written about the time period
options.b: Historical novels set during the time period studied
options.c: Documentaries that interview modern historians about the era
options.d: Letters, diaries, and photographs from the time period studied

distractorExplanations.a: Encyclopedias compile information after the fact, making them tertiary or secondary sources, not primary ones.
distractorExplanations.b: Historical fiction is a later creative work, even if well researched; primary sources are firsthand from the period.
distractorExplanations.c: Documentaries built on historians' commentary interpret the past, so they are secondary sources, not primary.

options.a: Convert map distances to real-world distances
options.b: Identify locations using latitude and longitude
options.c: Read elevation from color bands on the map
options.d: Find directions using the compass rose

distractorExplanations.b: Latitude and longitude come from the grid lines; a scale converts measured map distance into real distance.
distractorExplanations.c: Elevation is shown by contour lines or color bands with a key; the scale bar relates map length to ground distance.
distractorExplanations.d: The compass rose shows cardinal directions; the map scale is what converts inches on the map to miles.

options.a: Power is divided among three branches
options.b: States hold final authority over the nation
options.c: Government derives authority from the governed
options.d: Individual rights are protected from government

distractorExplanations.a: That is separation of powers, set out in Articles I-III; 'We the People' expresses popular sovereignty.
distractorExplanations.b: That reflects the Articles of Confederation approach; the Preamble grounds authority in the people of the nation.
distractorExplanations.d: Protecting individual rights is the Bill of Rights' focus; the Preamble's opening words signal popular sovereignty.

options.a: The form of government each one follows
options.b: The climate zone where each is located
options.c: The national laws that apply to residents
options.d: Population density and land use patterns

distractorExplanations.a: All three can share the same governmental structures; what distinguishes them is how densely land is settled and used.
distractorExplanations.b: Urban, suburban, and rural areas exist in every climate zone; they differ by population density and land use.
distractorExplanations.c: National laws apply equally across community types; the defining differences are density and land use.

options.a: Voting in elections from the age of 16
options.b: Obeying laws and participating in community
options.c: Serving in the military during peacetime
options.d: Joining a political party to vote in elections

distractorExplanations.a: The federal voting age is 18 under the 26th Amendment; voting at 16 is not a general responsibility of citizens.
distractorExplanations.c: Peacetime military service is voluntary in the U.S.; obeying laws and civic participation are general responsibilities.
distractorExplanations.d: Party membership is optional; citizens can vote in general elections without joining a party, so it is not a duty.

options.a: Locate historical events on a map according to their region
options.b: Compare population data across countries in a single year
options.c: Sequence events chronologically to see cause and effect
options.d: Group events by theme rather than date

distractorExplanations.a: Mapping events by place is a geography tool; timelines order events in time to reveal sequence and causation.
distractorExplanations.b: Population comparisons use tables or graphs; timelines arrange events chronologically to show relationships.
distractorExplanations.d: Thematic grouping sets chronology aside; timelines order events by date so cause and effect become visible.

options.a: Three articles of the U.S. Constitution
options.b: Seven articles of the U.S. Constitution
options.c: Ten articles of the Articles of Confederation
options.d: Ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution

distractorExplanations.a: Articles I-III establish the three branches; the Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791.
distractorExplanations.b: The Constitution's main body has seven articles; the Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments added in 1791.
distractorExplanations.c: The Articles of Confederation were the earlier national charter; the Bill of Rights amends the U.S. Constitution.

options.a: Equator and prime meridian
options.b: Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn
options.c: Arctic Circle and International Date Line
options.d: Latitude lines and time zone boundaries

distractorExplanations.b: The tropics bound the tropical zone; the equator splits north from south and the prime meridian splits east from west.
distractorExplanations.c: The Arctic Circle marks a polar zone; hemispheres are defined by the equator and the prime meridian at 0° longitude.
distractorExplanations.d: Time zones follow political borders, not hemisphere lines; the equator and prime meridian divide the hemispheres.

options.a: Celebrating cultures mainly through occasional holiday and food events
options.b: Including diverse perspectives and respectful discussion in curriculum
options.c: Treating every student the same by not discussing culture
options.d: Grouping students by cultural background for instruction

distractorExplanations.a: A 'heroes and holidays' approach is superficial; inclusive teaching weaves diverse perspectives into daily curriculum.
distractorExplanations.c: A color-blind approach ignores students' identities; inclusion means recognizing backgrounds through the curriculum.
distractorExplanations.d: Grouping by culture risks stereotyping and segregation; diverse perspectives should be shared across the whole class.

options.a: Printing currency and minting coins for circulation
options.b: Issuing passports and handling immigration cases
options.c: Police, fire protection, parks, and public schools
options.d: Regulating interstate commerce and highway trade

distractorExplanations.a: Currency is a federal power (Bureau of Engraving and Printing, U.S. Mint), not a local government service.
distractorExplanations.b: Passports and immigration are federal functions (State Department, USCIS); local governments run police, fire, parks.
distractorExplanations.d: Interstate commerce is regulated by Congress under the Commerce Clause; it is not a local government service.

options.a: Energy from producers to consumers
options.b: Matter from consumers back to producers
options.c: Energy from consumers to producers
options.d: Sunlight from herbivores to plants

distractorExplanations.b: Matter cycles back through decomposers, but a food chain's arrows show energy moving from producers to consumers.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the direction; energy flows from producers (plants) to the consumers that eat them, not backward.
distractorExplanations.d: Plants capture sunlight directly; herbivores eat plants, so energy passes from producers to consumers, not the reverse.

options.a: Aluminum, copper, and brass (metal materials)
options.b: Iron, nickel, and cobalt (magnetic materials)
options.c: Any metal, including gold and silver
options.d: Stainless steel of every grade and type

distractorExplanations.a: Aluminum, copper, and brass are metals but not ferromagnetic; magnets attract iron, nickel, and cobalt.
distractorExplanations.c: Not every metal is magnetic; gold and silver are not attracted, while iron, nickel, and cobalt are.
distractorExplanations.d: Some stainless grades (austenitic, such as 304) are barely magnetic; the reliably magnetic metals are iron, nickel, cobalt.

options.a: Movement from place to place, breathing air, and eating food
options.b: Cells with cell walls, chlorophyll, and photosynthesis
options.c: Growth, reproduction, response to environment, and use of energy
options.d: Growth by adding layers, as crystals and icicles do

distractorExplanations.a: Plants and many organisms do not move, breathe air, or eat; shared traits are growth, reproduction, response, energy use.
distractorExplanations.b: Cell walls and chlorophyll describe plants; animals lack them, so they are not characteristics shared by all life.
distractorExplanations.d: Crystals grow by accretion but are nonliving; growth alone does not mark life without reproduction and energy use.

options.a: Long-term average conditions; climate is day-to-day changes
options.b: Measured by temperature only; climate includes precipitation
options.c: Regional patterns over seasons; climate covers the whole globe
options.d: Short-term atmospheric conditions; climate is long-term patterns

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the terms: weather is short-term conditions, and climate is the long-term average over about 30 years.
distractorExplanations.b: Weather includes temperature, precipitation, wind, and humidity; the difference is timescale, not the variables.
distractorExplanations.c: Climate can be regional too; the distinction is short-term versus long-term, not local versus global scale.

options.a: All the populations of one species in an area
options.b: Living organisms and their nonliving environment interacting
options.c: The living community in an area, excluding abiotic factors
options.d: Nonliving factors such as soil, water, sunlight, and climate alone

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a population; an ecosystem includes all organisms plus nonliving factors like water and soil.
distractorExplanations.c: That is a community; an ecosystem adds abiotic factors such as sunlight, water, and soil interacting with organisms.
distractorExplanations.d: Abiotic factors by themselves are just the physical environment; an ecosystem is organisms and environment interacting.

options.a: Pumps blood throughout the body together with the heart muscle
options.b: Sends signals between the brain and the muscles
options.c: Protects internal organs and works with muscles for movement
options.d: Digests nutrients and absorbs them into the blood

distractorExplanations.a: Pumping blood is the heart's job in the circulatory system; the skeleton protects organs and enables movement.
distractorExplanations.b: Signaling is the nervous system's role; the skeleton protects organs and serves as levers that muscles pull.
distractorExplanations.d: Digestion and absorption belong to the digestive system; bones protect organs, store minerals, and enable movement.

options.a: Burning trash to generate electricity at waste-to-energy plants
options.b: Burying waste in lined landfills to stop leaks
options.c: Reusing materials to decrease resource extraction and landfill use
options.d: Shipping collected waste overseas for disposal in other countries

distractorExplanations.a: That is waste-to-energy incineration; recycling reprocesses used materials into new products to save resources.
distractorExplanations.b: Lined landfills contain waste safely but do not reduce it; recycling diverts materials away from landfills.
distractorExplanations.d: Exporting waste just moves it elsewhere; recycling reduces waste by turning used materials into new products.
